title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers deployed generative AI to create deepfakes and voice clones that impersonated real people, including a South Florida immigration attorney. The victims targeted were often immigrants and families vulnerable to emergency requests. This was a straightforward impersonation attack, enabled because deepfake technology could be used to clone voices and faces from public sources like social media with minimal investment by the attacker.

The failure happened at the point of initial contact. Victims had no way to verify that the person calling them or messaging them was who they claimed to be. The system was not deployed by the targets; it was deployed by criminals against them. Detection would have required either victims to independently verify requests through trusted channels before responding, or platforms and phone networks to implement authentication that made spoofing harder. It is not established whether social media platforms or phone carriers had tools in place to flag or block such impersonations.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence technology to create convincing deepfakes and voice clones that target victims across Georgia and South Florida. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report found that Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year, with criminals impersonating trusted individuals through fake voices, photos, and phone calls. In one case, a South Florida immigration attorney discovered criminals had cloned his voice to target immigrants, while a Cobb County couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints totaling nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia reported 71 complaints resulting in more than $10.4 million in losses.

Authorities say AI is making traditional scams far more believable by allowing criminals to clone voices from social media, spoof phone numbers, and research victims' family members. Common schemes include the AI grandparent scam, romance scams, and emergency distress calls. Banks are warning customers to verify unexpected requests through trusted channels before responding. Experts recommend establishing code words with family members, pausing before acting on urgent requests, and reporting suspected scams to law enforcement.
